title: a gift you didn't earn
hookLine: a gift you didn't earn; your grandmother said it before dinner
tomorrow: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town, not a stained-glass window

cards: The food is on the table, everybody's hungry, and somebody's grandmother says: wait. We haven't said grace. Heads go down.
A few words, maybe the same ones she's said every night for years. Then amen, and the forks move. Saying grace meant saying thanks.
But Christians use the word for something much larger: a gift you didn't earn.

teach.b: The Greek word in the New Testament is charis: a gift, a favor, kindness given freely. It's where English gets charisma, a gift someone just has. And it hides inside a word from day one: Eucharist, thanksgiving.

teach.h: IN GREEK, GIFT AND THANKS ARE KIN.
teach.b: In Greek, the gift and the thank-you belong to one family. Now the part that cuts against the grain. So much of life runs on earning.
You work, you get paid. You study, you pass. Grace doesn't work like that.
One of Paul's letters says it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not a wage. A gift.

Paul also describes a problem he begged the Lord three times to take away. He never says what it was. The answer he says he got was this: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
Enough, given right inside it. Churches have long argued about how grace reaches a person: through the sacraments, through faith, through both.
The word itself keeps its meaning: given, not earned. The grandmother at the table wasn't paying for dinner. She was saying: this came to us.

how: Many Christians say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals, and churches speak of grace as God's free gift, received in faith and, for many, through sacraments like baptism and communion.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a gift, a favor, freely given

s: grace is something you earn by being good
it means the opposite: a gift you didn't earn. "not of yourselves: it is the gift of God."
charis and Eucharist share a Greek root
charis, gift, sits inside eucharistia, thanksgiving.
Paul says God took his problem away
the answer he heard was "my grace is sufficient for thee." not removal: enough, inside it.

games.q: you're Paul. three times you beg God to take a problem away. what answer do you get?
games.why: "my grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." the problem stays. he never says what it was.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and notice your breathing. You didn't make this breath.
It just came, the way it's been coming all day while you weren't paying attention. Let each breath in be a gift you didn't earn. Let each breath out be a thank-you, said inside or not said at all.

wordCard.voice: Grace. Charis: a gift you didn't earn, freely given. Ninth word.

orig.note: Greek: gift, favor. the root of charisma, and hidden inside eucharistia, thanksgiving.

carryVoice: Your line: you are already held. That's what grace says, before anyone has earned anything. That's day nine.
